Even when regarded from a political point of view, the prophet’s advice was more likely to ensure peace than the king’s proposal, as the result of 2Ki 6:23 clearly shows. The Syrians did not venture any more to invade the land of Israel with flying parties, from fear of the obvious protection of Israel by its God; though this did not preclude a regular war, like that related in the following account. For אבי see the Comm. on 2Ki 5:13. וגו שׁבית האשׁר: “art thou accustomed to slay that which thou hast taken captive with sword and bow?” i.e., since thou dost not even slay those whom thou hast made prisoners in open battle, how wouldst thou venture to put these to death? כּרה להם יכרה, he prepared them a meal. כּרה is a <hi type="italic">denom</hi>. from כּרה, a meal, so called from the union of several persons, like <hi type="italic">coena</hi> from κοινή (vid., Dietr. on Ges. <hi type="italic">Lex. s. v</hi>. כרה).
entries.8413fc70ff36c0f144b7d46797701852297ebbff: 2Ki 6:24 <div eID="gen5210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5211" type="x-p"/> After this there arose so fearful a famine in Samaria on the occasion of a siege by Benhadad, that one mother complained to the king of another, because she would not keep her agreement to give up her son to be eaten, as she herself had already done.
entries.1e6c2d26f1df0980ce451a1ccb79baeeeecdd386: 2Ki 6:25 <div eID="gen5211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5212" type="x-p"/> The famine became great - till an ass’s head was worth eighty shekels of silver, and a quarter of a cab of dove’s dung was worth five shekels. היה בּ, to become for = to be worth. The ass was an unclean animal, so that it was not lawful to eat its flesh. Moreover the head of an ass is the most inedible part of the animal. Eighty shekels were about seventy thalers (£10, 10s. - Tr.), or if the Mosaic bekas were called shekels in ordinary life, thirty-five thalers (£5, 5s.; see Bertheau, <hi type="italic">Zur Gesch. der Isr. </hi>p. 49). According to Thenius, a quarter of a cab is a sixth of a small Dresden measure (<hi type="italic">Mässchen</hi>), not quite ten Parisian cubic inches. Five shekels: more than four thalers (twelve shillings), or more than two thalers (six shillings). The <hi type="italic">Chetbib</hi> חרייונים is to be read יונים, <hi type="italic">excrementa columbarum</hi>, for which the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> substitues the euphemistic יונים, <hi type="italic">fluxus</hi>, <hi type="italic">profluvium</hi> <hi type="italic">columbarum</hi>. The expression may be taken literally, since dung has been known to be collected for eating in times of terrible famine (vid., Joseph. <hi type="italic">Bell</hi>. <hi type="italic">Jud</hi>. v. 13, 7); but it may also be figuratively employed to signify a very miserable kind of food, as the Arabs call the <hi type="italic">herba</hi> <hi type="italic">Alcali</hi> Arab. <hi type="italic">s̆nân</hi>, i.e., sparrow’s dung, and the Germans call <hi type="italic">Asa</hi> <hi type="italic">foetida</hi> <hi type="italic">Teufelsdreck</hi>. But there is no ground for thinking of wasted chick-pease, as Bochart (<hi type="italic">Hieroz.</hi> ii. p. 582, ed. Ros.) supposes (see, on the other hand, Celsii <hi type="italic">Hierobot.</hi> ii. p. 30ff.).<note placement="foot">Clericus gives as a substantial parallel the following passage from Plutarch (<hi type="italic">Artax</hi>. c. 24): “he only killed the beasts of burden, so that the <hi type="italic">head of an ass</hi> was hardly to be bought for sixty drachmae;” and Grotius quote the statement in Plin. <hi type="italic">h. n.</hi> viii. 57, that when <hi type="italic">Casalinum</hi> was besieged by Hannibal a mouse was sold for 200 <hi type="italic">denaria</hi>.</note>
entries.0c393c68d7575aa1df959aee0303838bd1a55fb5: 2Ki 6:26 <div eID="gen5212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5213" type="x-p"/> As the king was passing by upon the wall to conduct the defence, a woman cried to him for help; whereupon he replied: אל־יושׁעך יי, “should Jehovah not help thee, whence shall I help thee? from the threshing-floor or from the wine-press?” It is difficult to explain the אל which Ewald (§355, <hi type="italic">b</hi>.) supposes to stand for אם לא. Thenius gives a simpler explanation, namely, that it is a subjective negation and the sentence hypothetical, so that the condition would be only expressed by the close connection of the two clauses (according to Ewald, §357). “From the threshing-floor or from the wine-press?” i.e., I can neither help thee with corn nor with wine, cannot procure thee either food or drink. He then asked her what her trouble was; upon which she related to him the horrible account of the slaying of her own child to appease her hunger, etc.
entries.733d03c9146f25ed33e4ac8881803704130fdec9: 2Ki 6:30 <div eID="gen5213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5214" type="x-p"/> The king, shuddering at this horrible account, in which the curses of the law in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.29">Lev 26:29</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.28.53">Deu 28:53</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.28.57">Deu 28:57</reference> had been literally fulfilled, rent his clothes; and the people then saw that he wore upon his body the hairy garment of penitence and mourning, מבּית, within, i.e., beneath the upper garment, as a sign of humiliation before God, though it was indeed more an <hi type="italic">opus operatum</hi> than a true bending of the heart before God and His judgment. This is proved by his conduct in 2Ki 6:31. When, for example, the complaint of the woman brought the heart-breaking distress of the city before him, he exclaimed, “God do so to me ... if the head of Elisha remain upon him to-day.” Elisha had probably advised that on no condition should the city be given up, and promised that God would deliver it, if they humbled themselves before Him in sincere humility and prayed for His assistance. The king thought that he had done his part by putting on the hairy garment; and as the anticipated help had nevertheless failed to come, he flew into a rage, for which the prophet was to pay the penalty. It is true that this rage only proceeded from a momentary ebullition of passion, and quickly gave place to a better movement of his conscience. The king hastened after the messenger whom he had sent to behead Elisha, for the purpose of preventing the execution of the murderous command which he had given in the hurry of his boiling wrath (2Ki 6:32); but it proves, nevertheless, that the king was still wanting in that true repentance, which would have sprung from the recognition of the distress as a judgment inflicted by the Lord. the desperate deed, to which his violent wrath had impelled him, would have been accomplished, if the Lord had not protected His prophet and revealed to him the king’s design, that he might adopt defensive measures.
entries.9e78d7ccfa49129231a60b5b3fa8e50a39b9fe3e: 2Ki 6:32 <div eID="gen5214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5215" type="x-p"/> The elders of the city were assembled together in Elisha’s house, probably to seek for counsel and consolation; and the king sent a man before him (namely, to behead the prophet); but before the messenger arrived, the prophet told the elders of the king’s intention: “See ye that this son of a murderer (Joram, by descent and disposition a genuine son of Ahab, the murderer of Naboth and the prophets) is sending to cut off my head?” and commanded them to shut the door against the messenger and to force him back at the door, because he already heard the sound of his master’s feet behind him. These measures of Elisha, therefore, were not dictated by any desire to resist the lawful authorities, but were acts of prudence by which he delayed the execution of an unrighteous and murderous command which had been issued in haste, and thereby rendered a service to the king himself. - In 2Ki 6:33 we have to supply from the context that the king followed close upon the messenger, who came down to Elisha while he was talking with the elders; and he (the king) would of course be admitted at once. For the subject to ויּאמר is not the messenger, but the king, as is evident from 2Ki 7:2 and 2 Kings 17. The king said: “Behold the calamity from the Lord, why shall I wait still further for the Lord?” - the words of a dispairing man, in whose soul, however, there was a spark of faith still glimmering. The very utterance of his feelings to the prophet shows that he had still a weak glimmer of hope in the Lord, and wished to be strengthened and sustained by the prophet; and this strengthening he received.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.6"/> <div eID="gen5215" type="x-p"/>

And the LORD opened their eyes, and they saw, and be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold <ns0:hi>they were</ns0:hi> in the midst of Samaria.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And the king of Israel <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To whom <ns0:hi>Elisha</ns0:hi> had doubtless sent notice of his In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tentions, that he might accordingly prepare himself.</ns0:note> said unto Elisha, when he saw them, My father <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Now he gives him this title of Reverence and Affection, because of a great and present benefit he received from him; though otherwise he hated him, and would not hearken to his Counsel.</ns0:note>, shall I smite them? shall I smite them <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The repetition of the question shews his great desire to smite them, and that with utter Destruction.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And he answered, Thou shalt not smite <ns0:hi>them:</ns0:hi> Wouldest thou smite those whom thou hast taken captive with thy sword, and with thy bow <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">It is against the Laws of Humanity, and Custom of War, to kill Captives, though thou thy self hast taken them with thy own Sword and Bow; which may seem to give thee some colour of Right to destroy them; but much more unworthy will it be in cold Blood to kill these, whom not thy Arms, but God's Miraculous Providence hath put into thy hands.</ns0:note>? set bread and water before them <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Give them Meat and Drink, which may refresh and strengthen them for their Journey. Which was an action of singular Piety and Charity, in doing good to their Enemies, which was much to the Honour of the True Religion; and of no less prudence, that hereby the hearts of the <ns0:hi>Syrians</ns0:hi> might be both mollified towards the <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> and afraid to Oppose that People who had such an Invincible Protector.</ns0:note>, that they may eat and drink, and go to their master.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And he prepared great provision for them, and when they had eaten and drunk, he sent them away <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Refreshed, but Disarmed, as is most probable.</ns0:note>, and they went to their master. So the bands of Syria came no more <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either 1. In such a manner, to wit, in small Bands, or Companies, which might be Entrapped, as these had been: but their next Attempt was, by an open and solemn War, and a Con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />junction of all their Forces, which they still ridiculously conceited would be too hard for the King, and Prophet, and God of <ns0:hi>Israel;</ns0:hi> notwithstanding their multiplied Experien<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces to the contrary. Or, 2. For some considerable time; until the Terror of these Examples was got out of their minds.</ns0:note> into the land of Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 ¶ And it came to pass after this, that Ben<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hadad king of Syria <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He whom <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi> wickedly and foolishly spared, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 20. 42. who now comes to requite <ns0:hi>Ahab's</ns0:hi> kindness, and to fulfil that Divine Prediction. <ns0:hi>Benhadad</ns0:hi> was a name ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry frequent among the Kings of <ns0:hi>Syria,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 15. 18, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> and Chap. 13. 24. 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 13. 3, 24. If not common to them all. See <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 49. 27. <ns0:hi>Amos</ns0:hi> 1. 4.</ns0:note> gathered all his host, and went up, and besieged Samaria.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 And there was a great famine in Samaria: and behold, they besieged it, until an asses head was <ns0:hi>sold</ns0:hi> for fourscore <ns0:hi>pieces</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Supposed to be Shekels; and the common Shekel being valued at fifteen pence of <ns0:hi>English</ns0:hi> Money, this amounts to five pounds. A vast price, especially for that which had on it so little Meat, and that unwholsome, and unclean by Law, <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 11. 13. though necessity might seem to excuse their violation of that Law.</ns0:note> of silver, and the fourth part of a kab <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">A measure containing 24 Eggs.</ns0:note> of doves dung <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which they used not for Fire (for he is speaking here one<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly of the scarcity of Food) but for Food. Which if it seem incredible, it must be considered, First, That Famine hath constrained People to eat things as improper and unfit for nourishment as this, as dry Leather, and Mans Dung, as is implied, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 36. 12. and affirmed by grave Historians. Se<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />condly, That some Creatures do usually eat the Dung of o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers. 3dly, That Doves Dung, though it be hotter than ordi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nary, might in other respects be fitter for nourishment than other, as being made of the best and purest Grains, and ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving some moisture in it, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Fourthly, That this <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> word being of an obscure and doubtful signification, and no where else used, may be, and is by Learned Men otherwise rendred and understood: either, first, of the Corn which is found in the Crops of Doves: or, secondly, of the Guts and other inwards of Doves: or rather, thirdly, of a sort of <ns0:hi>cicer</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>pease,</ns0:hi> which in the <ns0:hi>Arabick</ns0:hi> Language (which is near a kin to the <ns0:hi>Hebrew,</ns0:hi> and from which many words are explained), is called <ns0:hi>Doves Dung:</ns0:hi> for this was a Food much in use amongst the poorer <ns0:hi>Israelites,</ns0:hi> and was by all esteem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed a very course Food, and therefore fit to be joyned with an Asses head: and a <ns0:hi>kab</ns0:hi> was the usual Measure of all sorts of Grains and Fruits of that sort.</ns0:note> for five <ns0:hi>pieces</ns0:hi> of silver.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 And as the king of Israel was passing by up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on the wall <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To give necessary order for the Defence of the City a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gainst Assaults, and to see if the several Guards were watch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful and diligent, and if his directions were executed, and to observe the motions of the Enemy.</ns0:note>, there cried a woman unto him, say<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, Help my lord, O king.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And he said, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, Let <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> the Lord save thee.</ns0:note> If the LORD do not help thee <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>let not God help thee,</ns0:hi> as some both ancient and late Interpreters render the words. So they are words of Impatience, and Rage, and a formal Curse, wishing that God would not help her, as he could not, as <ns0:hi>Iosephus</ns0:hi> amongst o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers understand it: which agrees too well with the Cha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />racter of the Man, an Infidel, and Idolater, and a wicked Man, and at this time in a great Rage, as appears from <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 31. Or, they may be rendred thus, No; (as this <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Particle is sometimes used, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 20. 17. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 34. 5. and 41. 2. and 50. 3. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 3. 3, 25. and 31. 4.) <ns0:hi>let the Lord help thee.</ns0:hi> So it may be taken, Either, First, As a direction: No: do not cry to me; but to God for help: God help thee, for I cannot. Or rather, Secondly, As a prophane scoff. No: come not to me, but go to him to whom <ns0:hi>Elisha</ns0:hi> directs you; Pray to the Lord: you see how ready he is to help you, by his suffering you to come to this extremity: wait upon God for relief, as <ns0:hi>Elisha</ns0:hi> adviseth me: but I will wait no longer for him, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 33. and I will take a course with <ns0:hi>Elisha</ns0:hi> for thus abusing both me and my people with vain hopes. Or, thus, <ns0:hi>the Lord</ns0:hi> (on whom forsooth thou and I are commanded to wait for help) <ns0:hi>will not help thee,</ns0:hi> as he could easily do, and would do, if he were so good as <ns0:hi>Elisha</ns0:hi> pretends; <ns0:hi>whence</ns0:hi> then <ns0:hi>shall I help thee?</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, whence shall I help thee? out of the barn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />floor, or out of the wine-press <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Dost thou ask of me Corn or Wine, which I want for my self?</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 And the king said unto her, What aileth thee? And she answered, This woman said unto me, Give thy son, that we may eat him to day, and we will eat my son to morrow.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 So <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 28. 53, 57.</ns0:note> we boiled my son, and did eat him <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">A dreadful Judgment threatned to them in case of their Apostacy, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 28. 56, 57. in which they were now deep<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly plunged. Compare <ns0:hi>Ezek.</ns0:hi> 5. 10.</ns0:note>: and I said unto her on the <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                     </ns0:note> next day, Give thy son, that we may eat him: and she hath hid her son <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Either, that she might eat him alone; or rather, that she might save him from Death, her Bowels yearning towards him, and her hunger being in great measure satisfied.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 ¶ And it came to pass, when the king heard the words of the woman, that he rent his clothes <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Partly, in Grief for such an horrid Fact: and partly, through Indignation at the Prophet, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 31.</ns0:note>, and he passed by upon the wall, and the people <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Who were in great numbers upon the Wall, either to defend the City: or rather, to seek for relief from the Soldiers, for whose Provisions the King doubtless took special care, as it was necessary, for the preservation of the place.</ns0:note> looked, and behold, <ns0:hi>he had</ns0:hi> sackcloth within upon his flesh <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Under his in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ner Garments, in token of his sorrow, and with a pretence of humiliation, which he would shew by outward signs, as his Father <ns0:hi>Ahab</ns0:hi> had done, not without some advantage to himself, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 21. 27, 28, 29.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:306" />31 Then he said, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ruth 1. 17.</ns0:note> God do so, and more also to me, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat shall stand on him this day <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">If I do not this day take his head and life. This wretch<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed and partial Prince overlooks his own great and various sins, and amongst others his obstinate cleaving to the Ido<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />latry of the Calves, and the Whoredoms and Witchcrafts of his Mother <ns0:hi>Iezabel,</ns0:hi> 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 9. 22. and the Wickedness of his People, which was the true and proper cause of this and all their Calamities; and lays the blame of all upon <ns0:hi>Elisha,</ns0:hi> ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, supposing that he who had the Spirit of <ns0:hi>Elijah</ns0:hi> resting upon him, had brought this Famine by his Prayers, as <ns0:hi>Eli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />jah</ns0:hi> had formerly done, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 17. 1. or, because he had encouraged them to withstand the <ns0:hi>Syrians,</ns0:hi> by promising them help from God in due time: or, because he would not by his intercession to God, and the working of a Miracle, deliver them from these Calamities, as he easily could have done. But he did not consider, that the Prophets could not work what Miracles, and when they pleased, but onely as far as God saw fit, whose time was not yet come; otherwise it was <ns0:hi>Elisha's</ns0:hi> Interest as well as theirs to be freed from this distress.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 But Elisha sat in his house <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">In the House where he Iodged: for he had no House of his own, having forsaken all when he followed <ns0:hi>Elijah,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 19. 20, 21.</ns0:note> (and the el<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ders <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">So they might be called, Either, First, From their age. Or rather, Secondly, From their office, which was either Ecclesiastical, or Civil: so they were either the Sons of the Prophets: or rather, some Godly men who were then in some Power and Office, either in the Court, or Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />my, or City, as may seem probable from what he requires of them. And though <ns0:hi>Ioram</ns0:hi> was a wicked King, and most of his Officers probably like himself; yet there were some of them, whom <ns0:hi>Elisha's</ns0:hi> Holy Life, and Powerful Ministry, and Glorious Miracles, and the great and publick benefits pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cured by him, had won to God, and to the True Religion, at least to the profession of it, among which <ns0:hi>Iehu</ns0:hi> might be one: and these were here sitting with him; either, to receive comfort and counsel from him in this distressed time; or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther, to solicite him to use his Power with God, for their re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lief: which accordingly he doth, and in compliance with them, not out of any fear of the King, (from which he very well knew by frequent experience, and certain assurance, that God both could and would deliver him), he gives the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing answer, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 7. 1.</ns0:note> sat with him) and the king sent a man from before him <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>one</ns0:hi> of them who stood <ns0:hi>before his face,</ns0:hi> one of his Guard, or some other Officer, <ns0:hi>to take away his head,</ns0:hi> as it follows.</ns0:note>: but ere the messenger came to him, he said to the elders <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Being admonished by God of his danger.</ns0:note>, See ye how this son of a murderer <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The genuine Son of that wicked <ns0:hi>A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hab</ns0:hi> the Murderer of the Lords Prophets, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 18. 4. and 21. 9. whose <ns0:hi>son</ns0:hi> he is not by Birth onely, but also by his Man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners and Bloody disposition. Compare <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 8. 44. This ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression may seem very harsh and unfit; nor is it to be drawn into imitation by others: but it must be considered, that he was an extraordinary Prophet, intrusted with a Power in some sort superior to that of <ns0:hi>Ioram,</ns0:hi> and had Authority to controle and rebuke him in the Name of the King of kings.</ns0:note> hath sent to take away mine head <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To kill me, before he hear what I have to say.</ns0:note>? Look when the messenger cometh, shut the door, and hold him <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not the King, but the Messenger, who was last mentioned; that he may not break in upon me, and take away my life, before the King comes.</ns0:note> fast at the door: <ns0:hi>Is</ns0:hi> not the sound of his masters feet behind him <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">You shall not need to hold him long, for the King is just at his heels coming, as is probable; either, to recall his rash and furious sentence; or, at least to debate the matter with the Prophet, and to procure relief.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 And while he yet talked with them, behold, the messenger came down unto him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To wit, to the Door, where also we are to understand that he was held fast, that he could not come at the Prophet till the King came, as the Prophet had commanded them to do.</ns0:note>: and he said <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Either, 1. The Messenger in the Kings name and words. Or, Secondly, The King himself, who, though not here named, may be presumed to be present, both by the Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phets prediction of his speedy coming, and by the presence of the <ns0:hi>lord, on whose hand the king leaned,</ns0:hi> chap. 7. 2.</ns0:note>, Behold, this evil <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This dreadful Famine, which is now so extream, that Women are forced to eat their own Children.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> of the LORD <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He hath inflicted it, and (for ought that I see) he will net remove it. Thus he lays all the blame upon God, not, as he ought, upon his own, and his Mothers wickedness, which provoked God, who doth not willingly afflict, to send this heavy Judgment upon him.</ns0:note>, what should I wait for the LORD any longer <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Thou bidst me wait upon God for help: but I perceive I may wait long enough before deliverance comes: I am weary with waiting, I can wait no longer.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
